title: ₹50 Lakh FD for 5 Years: Senior Citizen Earnings in Small Finance Banks
description: Small Finance Banks (SFBs) often offer higher Fixed Deposit (FD) interest rates compared to larger commercial banks. Senior citizens typically receive an addi.

faq.q: What is a Small Finance Bank (SFB)?
faq.a: SFBs are a category of banks licensed by the RBI to provide basic banking services to underserved segments, offering deposits and loans. They often provide higher interest rates on FDs to attract deposits.

faq.q: How much more interest can a senior citizen earn on an FD?
faq.a: Senior citizens typically earn an additional 0.25% to 0.75% interest per annum on their Fixed Deposits compared to regular depositors. This can lead to significantly higher returns over the deposit tenure.

faq.q: Is the interest earned on an FD taxable?
faq.a: Yes, the interest earned on Fixed Deposits is fully taxable as "income from other sources" and is added to your total annual income for tax calculation. TDS may be deducted if interest exceeds certain thresholds.

faq.q: What is Form 15G/15H and when should I submit it?
faq.a: Form 15G (for non-senior citizens) and Form 15H (for senior citizens) are declarations submitted to the bank to request non-deduction of TDS if your total income is below the taxable limit. They should be submitted at the start of each financial year.

faq.q: Are Fixed Deposits in Small Finance Banks safe?
faq.a: Yes, Fixed Deposits in all RBI-licensed banks, including SFBs, are insured by the DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor, per bank, covering both principal and interest.

faq.q: Can I withdraw my FD before maturity?
faq.a: Most FDs allow premature withdrawal, but it usually comes with a penalty, such as a reduction in the interest rate by 0.50% to 1.00% from the contracted rate. It's best to check the specific bank's policy.

faq.q: What is the minimum age for a senior citizen FD?
faq.a: In India, an individual is generally considered a senior citizen for banking purposes if they are 60 years of age or above.
